rule: Went through shortlist.json in its fixed order. Each PR gets at most one question. Answerable = an author or reviewer states the reason for a decision in words; the first 15 such PRs are answerable, the next 3 are re-used as 'removed' (PR excluded from retrieval). After that, PRs were checked only for no-reason questions (a change the PR makes whose reason is not stated anywhere in the PR and does not follow from general knowledge); the first 5 are used. Skipped PRs and why are in selection_log.

questions.q: Why were short symbols such as V and M chosen as the y-axis labels of the beam plots instead of the full names of the quantities?
questions.a: Symbols take less space and make the plots neater, and the quantity's name is already shown in the title of each subplot.
quotes: +1 for using symbols, they will take lesser space and hence make the plot neater. Also, the name of the quantity in the y-axis will already be present in the title of the subplot.

questions.q: Why did the reviewer want Matrix.solve() to catch the singular case and raise a ValueError after it switched to Gauss-Jordan elimination?
questions.a: To preserve the existing behaviour: the old inverse-based solve raised an error for singular matrices, but Gauss-Jordan elimination does not, so catching that case keeps the error while still using the faster routine.
quotes: Because it is currently based on `inv` it raises an error when the matrix is singular. G-J won't do that so the changes I recommend catch that case and raise an error while still using a faster routine to calculate the solution.

questions.q: Why did the reviewers object to temporarily changing sympify's converters inside CodePrinter so that lists become List objects?
questions.a: Modifying a shared mutable object in place and reverting it afterwards is fragile and not thread-safe; the converters are only meant to be registered at start-up, so the conversion should be done explicitly instead.
quotes: This is also not thread-safe. The converters are only really supposed to be registered during start up.
importing a mutable object, modifying it in-place, calling a function using it, and then reverting the change

questions.q: Why was SparseMatrix extended to accept matrix-like values in its instantiation dictionary?
questions.a: It will be used to provide a simple way of instantiating banded matrices (as in #16180).
quotes: This will be used to provide a simple method of instantiating banded matrices as in #16180 .

questions.q: Why was it important that nsolve accept SymPy complex numbers as initial points?
questions.a: Because the default secant solver of mpmath's findroot will not find complex roots of real functions unless the initial point is non-real.
quotes: Worth noting that this is important because the secant solver of findroot (the default) won't find complex roots of real functions unless the initial point is nonreal.

questions.q: Why does the srepr printer's ordering option use the string 'none' rather than Python's None to turn ordering off?
questions.a: order=None already means that no ordering was given (use the default, e.g. 'lex'), whereas the string 'none' is the existing convention in the other printers for not reordering terms.
quotes: Having `order=None` means no ordering was provided rather than the "none" (aka don't reorder terms) ordering we are looking for.
IIRC `None` means use the default (which I think is `'lex'`) whereas `'none'` means no ordering (all the orderings are strings).

questions.q: Why had the contributor first put the fix for set equality into relational.py instead of adding equality handlers to the sets module?
questions.a: They had tried the handler approach first, but the two modules are so closely linked that they could not solve the resulting circular import.
quotes: Yes , thats what I tried at first but the two modules are so closely linked that their circular import issue couldn't be solved.

questions.q: Why did the reviewer say that principal_value() did not need separate code for the cases with zero or one singularity?
questions.a: If I is first computed from the end-point limits and kept, the loop over the singularities leaves it unchanged when there are none and also works when there is exactly one, so no special cases are needed.
quotes: The for-loop over the singularities list will not change the value of `I` if there are no singularities. The loop can also work when `n = 1`, so there is no need to add code for that case.

questions.q: Why was the default routine of solve_least_squares replaced with a call to solve?
questions.a: Because solve can use more efficient methods than computing an inverse, and it still includes the inverse method as an option.
quotes: I think `solve_least_squares` can make use of more efficient routines than computing inverses, and I simply replaced the default routine with solve, to make use of any linear solver implemented in and also by the fact that it already contains the naive inverse computation method.

questions.q: Why can CRootOf postpone computing its isolating intervals when the polynomial is irreducible, but not when it is composite?
questions.a: For an irreducible polynomial the root index n never needs adjusting, so the intervals can wait until they are needed; for a composite polynomial the index may need adjusting, which requires the intervals at construction time.
quotes: If `f` is irreducible, and you construct `CRootOf(f, n)`, then the index `n` need not be adjusted.
If `f` is irreducible, and you construct `CRootOf(f, n)`, then the index `n` need not be adjusted.

questions.q: Why did the reviewer prefer keeping doit()'s deep flag defaulting to True and passing deep=False only from __pow__?
questions.a: Most users don't know about the deep flag and call doit() expecting full simplification; defaults should be what end users expect, while library code can change them for its own uses.
quotes: The reason being that most people don't know about the deep flag, so they just call `doit()` expecting it to simplify the expression fully.

questions.q: Why did tensor contractions with replace_with_arrays give incorrect results before this fix?
questions.a: replace_with_arrays contracted the data arrays prematurely, before the metric had been applied.
quotes: Tensor contractions using `replace_with_arrays` would prematurely contract the data arrays before applying the metric

questions.q: In the code-quality fixes to prde.py, why did a reviewer ask for a removed minus sign to be kept?
questions.a: The minus sign comes from the pseudocode in the book that the code follows.
quotes: I would have preserved the minus sign here. It comes from the pseudocode in the book.

questions.q: Why were replace and bottom_up changed to use exact equality testing?
questions.a: They used a weaker equality test, so some replacements failed, for example replacing 0.5 with S.Half (1/2).
quotes: `replace` and `simplify.bottom_up` use weaker testing for equality, making replacements fail, e.g. `0.5 -> S.Half` fails.

questions.q: Why was get_relevant_facts() redesigned, with a new extract_predargs() function taking over part of its work?
questions.a: It had two completely different functionalities depending on whether exprs was passed, which made the design very confusing; extract_predargs now does the first and get_relevant_facts only the second.
quotes: In master, `get_relevant_facts()` has completely different two functionalities.
This design is very confusing.

questions.q: Why do Beam's slope() and deflection() methods now include integration constants such as C3 and C4?
questions.a: Integrating the bending moment twice without constants gave incomplete and sometimes misleading results; the constants mark the solution as incomplete when there are not enough boundary conditions.
quotes: This sometimes is misleading, hence constants are required to mark the incomplete solution.

questions.q: Why does continuous_domain find singularities by solving over the complex numbers and intersecting with the domain, rather than solving directly in the given domain?
questions.a: solveset gives inconsistent results for some functions such as 1/tan(x) (an empty set in bounded domains), so solving in the complex plane and intersecting with the domain avoids the problem.
quotes: the solveset returns an ImageSet union if the domain is `S.Complexes` or `S.Reals`, but returns an empty set in bounded domains like `Interval(0, pi)`.
Solving the function in the complex plain and taking the intersection with the domain solves this problem.

questions.q: Why did SymPy start refusing some substitutions inside a Derivative, such as replacing y with x in the derivative of f(x, y) with respect to y?
questions.a: Such a substitution produced Derivative(f(x, x), x), which is a different derivative, and this broke higher-order derivatives of expressions with undefined functions.
quotes: Currently, a substitution such as `Derivative(f(x, y), y).subs(y, x)` results in `Derivative(f(x, x), x)` which is a different derivative.
